title: Maximising the likelihood
objectives: Derive the maximum likelihood estimate for a coin and for a normal mean.
Check that a stationary point is a maximum, and check the boundaries.

screens.title: Where the slope is zero
screens.prose: A coin lands heads 7 times in 10 flips. Its likelihood is $L(p) = p^7(1 - p)^3$, drawn here 1000 times larger. The line at P is the tangent, labelled with its slope.
screens.question: Drag P to the top of the curve, where the tangent is flat.

hints.text: Is the slope positive or negative where P starts?
The slope changes sign between 0.6 and 0.8.
Drag P to $p = 0.7$. The slope there reads 0.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move P until the slope label reads 0.

byKey.half: You stopped near a fair coin. The slope there is still positive, so the curve is still rising.
byKey.P: The slope label is not 0 there yet. Move P towards the side where the curve is higher.

explain.text: You found the flat tangent at $p = 0.7$. Left of it the slope is positive, right of it negative, so this is the peak. That is 7 heads out of 10.

screens.prose: Change the data with the control: $k$ heads in 10 flips. Each curve is scaled so its peak height is 1, which keeps every shape visible.
screens.question: Try several values of $k$. Where is the peak each time?

options.text: At $p = k/10$, the share of heads

options.why: Set $k = 2$ and look: the peak moves left to 0.2. It follows the data.
That is a different estimate, with one extra head and tail added. The peak itself sits at $k/10$: check $k = 0$.
$k$ is a count from 0 to 10, but $p$ is a chance between 0 and 1. Divide by the 10 flips.

feedback.correct: The peak sits at the share of heads.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read off the peak for $k = 2$ and $k = 7$.

explain.text: The peak tracks the data: 0.2 for 2 heads, 0.7 for 7. At $k = 0$ and $k = 10$ it sits at the ends, 0 and 1. Next we prove the peak is always at $k/10$.

screens.title: The maximum likelihood estimate
screens.prose: The $p$ at the peak is the **maximum likelihood estimate**, written $\hat p$. To find it without sliding, differentiate. For 7 heads in 10, the product rule gives $L'(p) = 7p^6(1-p)^3 - 3p^7(1-p)^2$.
screens.question: Take out the common factor: $L'(p) = p^6(1-p)^2 \times (\;?\;)$. Enter the bracket.

hints.text: Both terms contain $p^6$ and $(1-p)^2$. What is left of each?
The first term leaves $7(1-p)$ and the second leaves $3p$. The tangent at the peak is flat.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each term by $p^6(1-p)^2$ and simplify.

byKey.no-expand: You left out the $(1 - p)$ from the first term. It leaves $7(1 - p)$, not 7.
byKey.sign: That is the bracket with the sign flipped. The first term is positive, so the bracket starts $7 - \dots$

explain.text: Taking out $p^6(1 - p)^2$ leaves $7(1 - p) - 3p = 7 - 10p$. The factor in front is positive for $0 < p < 1$. So $L'(p) = 0$ only when $7 - 10p = 0$, at $\hat p = 0.7$.

screens.prose: Now any data: $k$ heads in $n$ flips, with $0 < k < n$. Build the proof that $\hat p = k/n$, including the check that it is a maximum.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $L(p) = p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}$, the chance of the flips we saw
$L'(p) = k p^{k - 1}(1 - p)^{n - k} - (n - k) p^k (1 - p)^{n - k - 1}$, by the product and chain rules
$L'(p) = p^{k - 1}(1 - p)^{n - k - 1}\big[k(1 - p) - (n - k)p\big]$, taking out the common factors
$L'(p) = p^{k - 1}(1 - p)^{n - k - 1}(k - np)$, since $k - kp - np + kp = k - np$
The front factors are positive for $0 < p < 1$, so $L'(p) = 0$ only at $p = k/n$
$L' > 0$ below $k/n$ and $L' < 0$ above it, so $\hat p = k/n$ is the maximum

hints.text: Start from the likelihood, then differentiate it.
After differentiating, factor, then simplify the bracket.
The order is: likelihood, derivative, factor, simplify, solve, then check the sign on each side.

feedback.correct: Write, differentiate, factor, solve, check: $\hat p = k/n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must follow from the one above it.

byKey.m: The sign check uses $k - np$, so it comes after the zero is found.
byKey.z: You can only read off the zero once the bracket is simplified to $k - np$.

explain.text: The sign of $L'(p)$ is the sign of $k - np$: positive below $k/n$, negative above. So $L$ rises to $k/n$ and falls after it. The estimate is the share of heads, $\hat p = k/n$.

screens.prose: A new coin lands tails all 10 times, so $k = 0$. The likelihood is $L(p) = (1 - p)^{10}$, and $L'(p) = -10(1 - p)^9$.
screens.question: $L'(p)$ is never 0 for $0 < p < 1$. What is $\hat p$?

options.text: $\hat p = 0$, the end of the range
There is no MLE, because $L'(p) = 0$ has no solution
options.why: You only looked for a flat tangent. $L$ falls the whole way, so its highest point is the endpoint $p = 0$.

options.text: $\hat p = \tfrac{1}{10}$, since one head is the least we can allow
options.why: You added a head the data does not have. $L(0.1) = 0.35$, while $L(0) = 1$.
With 10 tails a fair coin has $L = 0.001$. The data points firmly to $p$ near 0.

hints.text: Is $L'(p)$ positive or negative between 0 and 1?
Where is the curve highest?
$L' < 0$ throughout, so $L$ falls from $L(0) = 1$. The highest point is the left end.

feedback.correct: The MLE can sit at a boundary: $\hat p = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the whole curve, ends included.

explain.text: $L'(p) < 0$ everywhere inside, so $L$ is largest at the left end, $p = 0$. That still matches $k/n = 0/10$. A boundary maximum has no flat tangent, so always check the ends.

screens.prose: A coin is known to favour tails, so $p \le 0.5$. It lands heads 7 times in 10. The solid part of the curve is the allowed range.
screens.question: What is the maximum likelihood estimate of $p$?

options.why: You set $L'(p) = 0$ and stopped. That root lies outside the allowed range, so it cannot be the estimate.

options.text: $\hat p = 0.5$, the edge of the allowed range

options.why: $L(0) = 0$, the lowest point. Checking the ends means comparing $L$ there, not taking either end.

options.text: No estimate exists in the range
options.why: $L$ rises across the whole allowed range, so it has a highest point there: the right edge.

hints.text: Inside $0 \le p \le 0.5$, is $L$ rising or falling?
$L'(p)$ has the sign of $7 - 10p$, which is positive for every allowed $p$.
$L$ climbs all the way to the edge, so compare $L(0) = 0$ with $L(0.5)$.

feedback.correct: $L$ rises up to the edge, so $\hat p = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the highest point of the solid curve.

byKey.root: You set $L'(p) = 0$ and stopped. That root lies outside the allowed range, so check where $L$ is largest inside it.

explain.text: Inside the allowed range $L'(p)$ has the sign of $7 - 10p$, which stays positive. So $L$ climbs to the edge, and $\hat p = 0.5$. A zero of $L'$ is only a candidate: check the ends and the sign.

screens.prose: Now a normal model. Three observations, 1.2, 2.0 and 3.7, come from a normal with $\sigma = 1$ and unknown mean $\mu$. Each stick is the density at one observation. The likelihood is their product.
screens.question: Slide $\mu$ to make the product as large as possible.

hints.text: Watch the caption. Where does the product stop rising?
The best $\mu$ keeps all three sticks reasonably tall.
Slide to 2.3, the average of 1.2, 2.0 and 3.7. The product peaks at 0.0124.

feedback.correct: The product peaks at $\mu = 2.3$, the average of the data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep sliding until the caption stops rising.

byKey.middle: You centred the curve on the middle observation, 2.0. The 3.7 pulls the best $\mu$ a little higher.

explain.text: The product peaks at $\mu = 2.3$, which is $(1.2 + 2.0 + 3.7)/3$. Moving right shortens the stick at 1.2 but lengthens the one at 3.7. The balance point is the sample mean.

screens.prose: Prove what you saw. Observations $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are independent draws from $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, with $\sigma$ known. Show that the MLE of $\mu$ is $\bar x$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $L(\mu) = C\, e^{-S(\mu) / (2\sigma^2)}$ with $S(\mu) = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2$, collecting constants into $C > 0$ and adding exponents
$L$ is largest where $S(\mu)$ is smallest, because $e^{-t}$ falls as $t$ rises
$S'(\mu) = -2\sum (x_i - \mu) = -2\big(\sum x_i - n\mu\big)$, by the chain rule on each square

hints.text: Start from the product of the densities.
Turn the product of exponentials into one exponential, then switch to minimising $S$.
Order: product, one exponential, minimise $S$, differentiate $S$, solve, check $S'' > 0$.

feedback.correct: The MLE of a normal mean is the sample mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must use only what the lines above it give.

byKey.e: You need $L$ written as one exponential of $S(\mu)$ before you can switch to minimising $S$.
byKey.m: The second-derivative check comes after the zero of $S'$ is found.

explain.text: Maximising $L$ is the same as minimising $S(\mu) = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2$. Its derivative vanishes at $\bar x$, and $S'' = 2n > 0$ confirms a minimum of $S$. The known $\sigma$ never enters the answer.

screens.prose:
Both times you followed one recipe. Write $L(\theta) = \prod f(x_i \mid \theta)$. Solve $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = 0$ for $\theta$, not for the data. Then check the sign either side, and the ends of the range.

$$\hat p = \frac{k}{n}, \qquad \hat\mu = \bar x$$
screens.question: Four observations, 2, 3, 4 and 11, come from a normal with known $\sigma$. What is $\hat\mu$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The derivation gave $\hat\mu = \bar x$.

byKey.median: You took the middle value, the median. The normal likelihood is maximised by the mean, which the 11 pulls up.
byKey.sum: You added the observations but did not divide by $n = 4$.

explain.text: The recipe gave $\hat\mu = \bar x$, so $\hat\mu = 20/4 = 5$. The 11 pulls it above the median of 3.5. Squared distances weigh far observations heavily.

screens.title: A strategy's track record
screens.prose: A strategy won 23 of its 40 trades. Its daily returns over its first week are in the table. Model wins as independent with chance $h$, and daily returns as normal with mean $\mu$ and a known sd.
screens.question: Fill in the two maximum likelihood estimates.

hints.text: Both are recipes you derived: a share for the wins, a mean for the returns.
$\hat h = k/n$ with $k = 23$, $n = 40$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\hat h = k/n$ and $\hat\mu = \bar x$.

explain.text: The hit rate is $k/n = 23/40 = 0.575$. The mean return is $1.2/5 = 0.24\%$ a day. Five days is very little data, as level 3 will make precise.

screens.title: Trades per minute
screens.prose: Trades arrive in a quiet stock at a rate of $\lambda$ per minute. A Poisson model gives $P(X = x) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x / x!$. For the six minutes in the table, $L(\lambda) = C\, e^{-6\lambda}\lambda^{24}$, where $C$ does not depend on $\lambda$.
screens.question: Differentiate, set $L'(\lambda) = 0$, and give $\hat\lambda$.

hints.text: Use the product rule on $e^{-6\lambda}\lambda^{24}$.
$L'(\lambda) = C\lambda^{23}e^{-6\lambda}(24 - 6\lambda)$.
The front factors are positive for $\lambda > 0$, so $24 - 6\lambda = 0$.

feedback.correct: $\hat\lambda = 4$ trades per minute, the mean count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Factor $L'(\lambda)$ and find where the bracket is zero.

byKey.total: That is the total count. The rate is per minute, so divide by the 6 minutes.
byKey.minutes: That is the number of minutes. The rate is total trades over minutes.

explain.text: $L'(\lambda) = C\lambda^{23}e^{-6\lambda}(24 - 6\lambda)$ is zero at $\hat\lambda = 4 = \bar x$, positive below and negative above. Check: $L(5)/L(4) = 0.52$ and $L(3)/L(4) = 0.40$. For a Poisson sample, the MLE of the rate is the sample mean.

ideas: The maximum likelihood estimate $\hat\theta$ is the parameter value at the peak of $L(\theta)$.
Find it by solving $L'(\theta) = 0$ for the parameter, then check the sign either side and the ends.
For a coin $\hat p = k/n$; for a normal mean $\hat\mu = \bar x$; for a Poisson rate $\hat\lambda = \bar x$.

formula.name: MLE of a coin's chance
formula.note: From $L'(p) \propto k - np$, positive below $k/n$ and negative above.

summary.trap: A zero of $L'$ is only a candidate. A boundary such as $p = 0$, or the edge of an allowed range, can be the maximum.

quiz.prose: A strategy wins 18 of 30 trades, each independently with chance $h$.
quiz.question: What is $\hat h$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\hat h = k/n$.

byKey.odds: You divided wins by losses, $18/12$. That is the odds; the chance divides by all 30 trades.
byKey.count: That is the number of wins. A chance divides it by the 30 trades.

explain.text: The MLE is the share of wins: $\hat h = 18/30 = 0.6$.

quiz.prose: For 7 heads in 10 flips, $L(p) = p^7(1 - p)^3$. A student treats the count 7 as the variable and differentiates with respect to it.
quiz.question: What should be differentiated, and with respect to what?

options.text: $L$, with respect to the parameter $p$, with the data held fixed
$L$, with respect to the data, since the data varies
options.why: The data is already observed and fixed. We ask which $p$ best explains it, so $p$ is the variable.

options.text: $L$ with respect to $p$ and the count, set both to zero
options.why: The count is not a free choice: it is what you saw. Only $p$ moves.

options.text: The chance of $p$, with respect to the data
options.why: $L$ is not a distribution over $p$. We maximise $L$ itself over $p$.

feedback.correct: The data is fixed; the parameter moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which quantity is unknown.

explain.text: The likelihood is a function of the parameter with the data fixed. So we differentiate with respect to $p$ and solve for $p$.

quiz.prose: Four observations, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 and 0.5, come from a normal with $\sigma = 2$ known.
quiz.question: What is $\hat\mu$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The known $\sigma$ does not enter $\hat\mu$.

byKey.sigma: You multiplied by $\sigma$. The known $\sigma$ drops out: $\hat\mu$ is just the mean.
byKey.n-1: You divided by $n - 1 = 3$. The MLE of the mean divides by $n$.

explain.text: $\hat\mu = \bar x = (1.5 + 2.5 + 3.5 + 0.5)/4 = 2$. The value of $\sigma$ scales $L$ but does not move its peak.

quiz.prose: A Poisson model for trades per minute. Five minutes show 1, 0, 2, 0 and 2 trades.
quiz.question: What is $\hat\lambda$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The MLE of a Poisson rate is the mean count.

byKey.total: That is the total. Divide by the 5 minutes.
byKey.nonzero: You dropped the quiet minutes. A minute with no trades is data too.

explain.text: $L(\lambda) \propto e^{-5\lambda}\lambda^5$, which peaks at $\hat\lambda = 5/5 = 1$. The two empty minutes count: they pull the rate down.
